payload.rationale: No current data were supplied, so this rests on background knowledge through early 2026 plus transfer assumptions. Observed facts (as of my knowledge): 2025 ended with roughly 2,000+ confirmed US measles cases, the most since 1992; large outbreaks in South Carolina and Utah/Arizona carried high transmission into early 2026, with several hundred cases per month reported in January–March 2026, putting 2026 on pace to exceed 2025 well before mid-year. Uncertain/assumed: I do not know the CDC count as of September 2026. Extrapolating a winter–spring pace of ~400–700 cases/month with a typical summer/fall slowdown suggests a September cumulative somewhere around 3,000–5,000, leaving a substantial gap to 6,000 with only ~3.5 months remaining, during which measles activity is usually seasonally lower (though the late-2025 outbreaks show winter surges are possible). Reaching >6,000 would require sustained ~500+/month or a new large under-vaccinated-community outbreak (e.g., Texas-2025 scale) in Q4. Too low risk: if the spring 2026 count actually ran higher than I assume (e.g., 4,500–5,500 by September, or the US formally lost elimination status amid uncontrolled spread), 6,000 becomes likely; CDC counting also includes cases later reclassified, and reporting lags can add cases in December. Too high risk: measles surges typically burn out in affected communities after vaccination campaigns; fall incidence in 2025 was much lower than spring; and a September count near 3,000 would make 6,000 nearly unreachable. Net estimate ~25%.
limitations: No supplied evidence or current CDC counts for 2026; September 2026 cumulative total unknown.
Estimate relies on memory of early-2026 outbreak pace, which may be inaccurate.
Seasonal pattern and outbreak burnout assumptions are transfer assumptions, not observations.
CDC weekly updates and revision timing relative to contract expiration could affect the counted figure.
